  • Social consequences: In modern dating, transparency is increasingly valued, and overt deception can backfire in a culture where authenticity is prized.

The line between strategic deception and manipulation depends on:

  • Intent: Is the goal mutual benefit (e.g., both parties enjoy the encounter) or one-sided exploitation?

If a man wants long-term success without deception, research suggests:

  • Authentic self-presentation: Women often prefer honesty in the long run, as it reduces relationship maintenance costs.
  • Social proof through real achievements: Instead of faking status, earning it (e.g., career growth, hobbies) makes deception unnecessary.

For men who prefer long-term success, genuine social skills and resourcefulness often prove more reliable than deception. But for those in competitive mating markets, strategic misrepresentation remains a time-tested (if ethically questionable) approach.
